# Overview of the National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI) - ECCC webinar

> **Provenance note:** This file comes from the publisher's web page (canada.ca), not from Brightspace. Verbatim retrieval was not possible through the available fetch tool (it returned a detailed paraphrase only), so the text below is a faithful point-by-point **paraphrase of the published transcript**. It is not verbatim. The page notes some video content may not reflect the latest updates (the video dates from 2017; current
figures are in [../../course/npri.md](../../course/npri.md)).

**Topics:** what the NPRI is and why it exists, who reports, requirements, substances, what is reported, data users,
timeline, facility support, data access and products, what data can show, how requirements changed.

**What it is:** Canada's inventory of releases to air, water and land, and disposals and transfers for treatment and
recycling. Established 1993; data from 1993 to the latest year; about 7,500 facilities; more than 300 pollutants
(toxic substances, smog and acid-rain air pollutants, other pollutants of concern).

**Why:** mandated (including publication) under CEPA 1999; key tool for identifying and monitoring pollution sources;
public right to know; encourages reductions, improves understanding, informs government programs.

**Who reports:** industrial facilities (oil and gas extraction, forest products mills, refineries, mines, chemical
manufacturers), waste management, municipal wastewater treatment, electric power generation, airports, some federal
departments (e.g. National Defence). Exempt: agriculture, forestry, oil and gas exploration and drilling. Not every
facility in a reporting sector reports.

**Requirements:** published every two years in Canada Gazette Part I; mandatory survey; report if employees equal 10
full-time workers or listed activities (incineration, municipal sewage treatment) and substance quantities exceed
thresholds; penalties under CEPA for non-reporting; year-round helpdesk.

**Substances:** >300 incl. asbestos, bisphenol A, benzene; mercury, lead; PAHs; dioxins and furans; sulphur dioxide,
carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides. Groups with their own criteria (quantity manufactured/processed/used, released, or
activity-based). Full list on the website.

**What is reported:** quantities released (air, surface water, land - by type, e.g. stack emissions, spills and leaks,
direct discharges), disposed (on/off-site: landfill, land application, underground injection, mine tailings, waste
rock), transferred off-site for recycling or treatment (type and destination); facility ownership, location, sector;
substance use, pollution prevention activities, reasons for changes; optional comments.

**Users:** governments and international organizations, industry associations, companies, media, academics,
students, NGOs, public.

**Timeline:** requirements published every two years (winter); online reporting opens in March; deadline June 1 for
the previous calendar year; review; preliminary data in early July (draft - do not use for analysis); summary report
and reviewed data published in December in several formats.

**Support:** website guidance, FAQs, video tutorials; Toolbox (estimation methods, calculators, external links);
helpdesk by phone/email.

**Data access:** NPRI website and Open Data portal; online query site (by facility, substance, location); predefined
queries (by province, industry, substance); latest-year Google Earth map layer; downloads as .csv, Excel or Access for
custom and multi-year analysis.

**What data show:** releases/disposals/transfers for the latest year and trends; pollutant profiles for sectors,
provinces, cities; releases near your home; pollution prevention activities; annual summary report.

**Changes:** anyone can propose changes (add/delete substances, change thresholds), assessed under "Process for
proposing and considering changes to the NPRI", consulted with the NPRI Multi-Stakeholder Work Group and posted for
public comment. Over 150 substances added since the start; more facilities report due to tightened requirements and
removed exemptions (graph of substances added vs facilities reporting). Consider these changes when analysing data.
